details:
Our project, Cosmicare, is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring system that we developed to help astronauts understand and manage their health during long space missions, especially missions to Mars, where communication with Earth can take a long time.

The main idea behind Cosmicare is to make medical monitoring more accessible and easier for astronauts, even if they don't have much medical knowledge. Our website monitors different physiological systems, including the cardiovascular, skeletal, neurological, respiratory, gastrointestinal, and integumentary systems. It displays health measurements, changes over time, and interactive 3D anatomical models to help astronauts visualize what is happening in their bodies.

One of the most important features we developed is the integration of Google Gemini AI. Instead of analyzing only one reading, the AI can analyze the last 5–10 minutes of recorded data, compare trends, and generate medical assessments based on the available information. It can also suggest daily routines, medical checks, and missions that astronauts should complete. We added interactive guides for these tasks, with illustrations and step-by-step explanations, because we wanted the system to be understandable even for someone without medical experience.

We also developed different astronaut simulation profiles, such as healthy astronauts and astronauts with higher monitoring needs, to test how the system responds to different situations. The website records data with timestamps, allowing previous readings and completed missions to be considered in future AI assessments. We also included NASA research datasets to support our project and explore how real space biology research can be connected to astronaut health monitoring.

For the development, we used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Three.js, and Python. We used Google Gemini API for AI analysis, and ChatGPT assisted us with coding, debugging, and improving the design. The project currently runs locally using a Python server, and we didn't use physical medical sensors, so the physiological readings are simulated rather than collected from real astronauts.

What makes Cosmicare different, in our opinion, is that we didn't want to create just another dashboard showing numbers and graphs. We wanted to make a system that can actually explain what those numbers might mean, suggest what should be checked next, and help astronauts organize their medical routines. We also separated current physiological assessments from long-term spaceflight exposure risks, since being exposed to microgravity doesn't automatically mean that an astronaut is unhealthy.

While developing the project, we considered things like ease of use, communication delays, astronaut safety, data accuracy, and the limitations of AI. We made it clear that the AI suggestions are not confirmed medical diagnoses and that real medical decisions still require qualified professionals.

Our goal is that Cosmicare could eventually become part of a more advanced autonomous health monitoring system for space missions. We know that our current version is still a prototype and needs much more testing, but we believe it shows how AI could help astronauts become more independent when medical support from Earth is limited.
